Brute-force protection__TRILIUM_PH_0__

Trilium limits each IP address to 10 failed sign-in attempts in 15 minutes. Once an address reaches the limit, Trilium rejects every further attempt from it, including correct ones, until the 15 minutes have passed. The sign-in page then shows __TRILIUM_PH_0__Too many login attempts__TRILIUM_PH_1__; other clients receive HTTP status 429.
The limit applies to every way of signing in with the password:
The sign-in page.
Setting up __TRILIUM_PH_0__Synchronization__TRILIUM_PH_1__ from a desktop or mobile app.
Connecting the __TRILIUM_PH_0__Web Clipper__TRILIUM_PH_1__ or the Android sender app.
Requesting a token through __TRILIUM_PH_0__ETAPI (REST API)__TRILIUM_PH_1__.
All of these count toward the same limit, and a wrong password, a wrong one-time password and a wrong recovery code each count as one failed attempt. Successful sign-ins are not counted.
The limit is per IP address, not per account, so an attacker cannot lock you out by failing to sign in from their own address. The count is kept in memory: restarting the server clears it.

Behind a reverse proxy, Trilium sees every request as coming from the proxy unless it is configured as a __TRILIUM_PH_0__Trusted proxy__TRILIUM_PH_1__. All clients then share a single limit, so a few wrong attempts from anyone block everyone.

Tools such as fail2ban can match either the log line or the 401 responses to __TRILIUM_PH_3__ in the reverse proxy's access log to block an address for longer than 15 minutes.

units.source: Understanding how the session works__TRILIUM_PH_0__
units.context: Authentication > Understanding how the session works

units.source: Once logged into Trilium, the application will store this information about the login into a cookie on the browser, but also as a session on the server.
units.context: Authentication > Understanding how the session works

units.source: If “Remember me” is checked, then the login will expire in 21 days. This period can be adjusted by modifying the __TRILIUM_PH_0__ value in __TRILIUM_PH_1__. For example, to have the session expire in one day:
units.context: Authentication > Understanding how the session works

units.source: When “Remember me” is unchecked, the behavior is different. At client/browser level the authentication does not have any expiration date, but it will be automatically cleared as soon as the user closes the browser. Nevertheless, the server will also dismiss this authentication in around 24 hours from the __TRILIUM_PH_0__last interaction with the application__TRILIUM_PH_1__.
units.context: Authentication > Understanding how the session works

units.source: Changing or resetting the password logs out every session, including the one that made the change: open tabs return to the login screen, where you log in again with the new password. This also applies when the password is changed on another instance and reaches the server through synchronization.
units.context: Authentication > Understanding how the session works

units.source: Changing the password does not revoke __TRILIUM_PH_0__ETAPI (REST API)__TRILIUM_PH_1__ tokens. They are separate credentials for scripts and integrations, and they keep working until you delete them. If you suspect that someone has obtained your session cookie, change the password, then go to __TRILIUM_PH_2__Options__TRILIUM_PH_3__ → __TRILIUM_PH_4__ETAPI__TRILIUM_PH_5__ and delete any token you don't recognize by its name and __TRILIUM_PH_6__Created__TRILIUM_PH_7__ date, since anyone with your session can create new tokens.
units.context: Authentication > Understanding how the session works
